 Lake Hefner and Lake Overholster see rising water levels after recent rainfall
 After months of a drought and extremely low water levels, recent rainfall is helping Oklahoma City lakes and welcoming back recreational water activities.
 Miracle Garrett 
 October 15, 2026 07:14 PM 1 min read 
 Lake Hefner and Lake Overholster see rising water levels after recent rainfall
 After months of a drought and extremely low water levels, recent rainfall is helping Oklahoma City lakes and welcoming back recreational water activities.
 OKLAHOMA CITY - Recent rainfall is bringing water levels up at Lake Hefner and Lake Overholster after months of sitting below full elevation. 
 Just over two weeks ago, the shoreline of Lake Hefner could be seen as dry, exposed dirt. Residents of Oklahoma City have reported the lake so shallow, you could walk across the water where boats normally sit. 
 Shawn Cina, incoming commodore of the Oklahoma City Boating Club, said the low water levels completely stopped the sailing season.
 “We had to stop sailing in August. Eventually, there’s just not enough water,” Cina said.
 Cina, who has been boating in Oklahoma City for years, said he remembers similarly low water levels in 2011.
 “When you see the harbor with where there’s normally boats and you can walk across it, it’s really bad looking,” he said.
 How much rain did Oklahoma receive?
 Parts of the Oklahoma City metro received several inches of rain, while some areas west of the city saw more than a foot, according to News 9 meteorologist David Payne.
 Payne said it will take several days for runoff to move through streams and rivers before reaching lakes, meaning water levels could continue rising.
 As of Thursday, Lake Overholser was 2.72 feet below full elevation, while Lake Hefner was 5.01 feet below full elevation, according to Jasmine Morris, public information manager for OKC Utilities.
 The additional water is great news for boaters such as Dylan Andrews, a city sailor who operates sailing charters with Island Rhythm Adventures.
 Andrews said the low water levels forced the business to cancel services beginning in August. With water levels rising, he is ready to return to the lake.
 “We’re back in business, baby, I’m 100% ready to get back out on the water.” Andrews said.
 The effects of low water levels extend beyond sailing. Cina said Lake Hefner supports kayakers, fishermen, power boaters and visitors to nearby restaurants.
 He said the lake also provides beautiful views and popular sunset photos.
 Payne said the rainfall benefits more than lakes. It can also replenish underground aquifers that supply water through wells.
 Is the drought over?
 While the rain has helped ease drought conditions, Payne said it will take about 12-15 inches of rainfall across much of Oklahoma to end the drought completely.
 Miracle Garrett 
 I am an Oklahoma native from Owasso, Oklahoma. I graduated from the University of Central Oklahoma with a Bachelor of Arts in Mass Communication for professional media and a minor in Journalism.
